content.title: About
content.content: Farro is a whole grain of ancient wheat (Triticum dicoccum) often referred to as “spelt” or “emmer wheat.” Pearled farro has had its outer husk removed, which shortens cooking time while retaining most of its nutrients. It offers a nutty, slightly sweet flavor and a firm, chewy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Farro is one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.
Pearled farro cooks faster than whole farro but still preserves a high nutrient content.
Compared with modern wheat varieties, farro contains less gluten, making it more tolerable for some gluten‑sensitive individuals.
It is a staple in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines, used in salads, soups, and side dishes.
Farro seeds can be sprouted, producing nutritious sprouts for salads and smoothies.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Pearled farro provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Good source of plant protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of dry farro contains about 14 g of protein, making it a valuable protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Contains magnesium and iron
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function, while iron is essential for hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Farro raises blood glucose slowly, which can help with weight management and diabetes control.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: The grain is rich in phenolic compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten sensitivity
items.content: Although farro has less gluten than common wheat, it can still trigger reactions in people with celiac disease.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Like many whole grains, farro contains phytic acid, which may reduce mineral absorption if consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Cereal allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to grains, including farro.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Farro can be boiled like rice or couscous, added to salads, soups, stews, and casseroles. Rinse the grains and optionally soak for 1–2 hours to shorten cooking time. It also works well in cold salads after cooking until tender and cooling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry farro in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.
